title: Sweaty and muddled in the waiting room

banner.text: She is confused and slow to answer.

brief.situation: 11:00 in a family practice. Mrs. Abara, 78, here for a routine diabetes visit, is sweaty, trembling and muddled in the waiting room. Her daughter says she skipped breakfast.
handover: Type 2 diabetes, last A1C 6.4%; chronic kidney disease. She can swallow and follow simple directions.
The office has glucose tablets, glucagon, a glucometer and a staff kitchen.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Treat what is in front of you, check that it worked, and find out why it happened.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. The visit ends an hour in, then a debrief scores what you did.

cues.question: What happened to Mrs. Abara, and what has to change so it does not happen again?

parts.label: Recognize and treat
parts.criteria: Names level 2 hypoglycemia (52 mg/dL) with symptoms; treats with 15 g glucose by mouth while she can swallow, rechecks in 15 minutes and repeats if still below 70, then gives a meal; glucagon only if she cannot swallow.
parts.modelAnswer: A glucose of 52 with sweating and confusion is level 2 hypoglycemia. She can swallow, so 15 g of glucose now, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still under 70, then a meal with starch and protein once she is above 70. Glucagon is for someone who cannot take sugar by mouth.

parts.label: Why and what changes
parts.criteria: Links it to the doubled sulfonylurea with reduced kidney function, a skipped meal and an A1C below her likely target; stops or replaces the sulfonylurea with a lower-risk choice and follows up soon; does not send her home while low.
parts.modelAnswer: Her glipizide was doubled, her kidney function is reduced, she skipped breakfast, and her A1C of 6.4% is tighter than a frail 78-year-old needs; she has had other spells. Stop the glipizide, relax her target, choose an agent with a low hypoglycemia risk, teach meter use and call in two days. She does not leave until her glucose is above 70 and she has eaten.

wentLow.body: A plan is not treatment. She needed a glucose above 70 and a meal before leaving.

fixedTarget.headline: Treated, confirmed and prevented
fixedTarget.body: 15 g, a recheck at 15 minutes, a meal, and the sulfonylurea stopped. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: A glucose of 52 mg/dL with sweating and confusion is level 2 hypoglycemia. While she can swallow, give 15 g of glucose, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still below 70; once above 70, give a meal with starch and protein. Glucagon is for someone who cannot take carbohydrate by mouth; chocolate's fat slows absorption. Then find the cause: a doubled glipizide dose with reduced kidney function, a skipped meal and an A1C tighter than a frail older adult needs. Stop the sulfonylurea, relax the target, choose a lower-risk agent and follow up soon. She does not leave while low.

gQ.ask: Her glucose is coming up. Is the problem solved?

choices.label: Yes, the glucose tablets fixed it
No: the drug that caused it is still working; feed her and change the regimen

gQ.explain: Glucose tablets treat the episode; a meal holds the glucose up; and the cause (here a doubled glipizide dose with reduced kidney function) has to change or it will recur.
